Estimate the split-half reliability of a lag transition network

Source: R/reliability_lsa.R
reliability_lsa.Rd

reliability_lsa() estimates the split-half reliability of a lag transition network from one data set. A lag transition network is reliable when two independent samples of the same population give similar networks. Split-half reliability follows the resampling approach that Epskamp, Borsboom and Fried (2018) describe for the accuracy of psychological networks: the sequences are divided at random into two halves, a network is estimated on each half, and the two networks are compared transition by transition. A high correlation between the halves means that the structure of the network does not depend on which sequences happened to be sampled.

The random split is repeated R times. Each split assigns half of the sequences to one half and the rest to the other, refits the model on each with the same engine and settings, and correlates the two halves' transition probabilities, counts or adjusted residuals over all transitions. reliability_lsa() reports the mean, standard deviation and 95% interval (2.5% and 97.5% quantiles) of the split-half correlations, and the number of failed replicates, in which a half had no transitions or a half's values did not vary. A grouped fit gives one result per group.

Reliability describes the network as a whole. For the precision of each transition use bootstrap_lsa() or certainty_lsa(); for whether each transition stays significant when sequences are dropped, use stability_lsa().

Usage

reliability_lsa(fit, ...)

# S3 method for class 'lsa'
reliability_lsa(
  fit,
  R = 100L,
  weights = c("prob", "count", "adj_res"),
  method = c("pearson", "spearman"),
  parallel = FALSE,
  n_cores = NULL,
  verbose = FALSE,
  ...
)

# S3 method for class 'lsa_group'
reliability_lsa(fit, ...)

# S3 method for class 'lsa_reliability_group'
print(x, ...)

# S3 method for class 'lsa_reliability'
print(x, ...)

Arguments

fit

An lsa fit from lsa(), or a grouped fit from lsa(..., group = ), built from at least two sequences (not from a transition matrix).

...

For a grouped fit, the arguments above, passed on to each group; otherwise not used.

R

Number of random splits. Default 100.

weights

Transition values correlated between the halves: "prob" (default, transition probabilities), "count" or "adj_res" (adjusted residuals).

method

Correlation: "pearson" (default) or "spearman".

parallel

Run the splits on several cores. Default FALSE.

n_cores

Number of cores when parallel = TRUE. Default NULL, all cores but one.

verbose

Report progress every 100 splits. Default FALSE.

x

An lsa_reliability or lsa_reliability_group object, for the print() methods.

Value

An object of class c("lsa_reliability", "list"). Read it with as.data.frame(): as.data.frame(x) gives one row per split with its correlation (NA for a failed replicate), and as.data.frame(x, what = "summary") one row with the settings, the number of failed replicates n_failed, and the mean, sd, ci_low and ci_high of the correlations. print() shows the same summary and returns x invisibly. For a grouped fit, an object of class c("lsa_reliability_group", "list") with one result per group, whose tables gain a leading group column.

Conditions

Errors carry the class lagdynamics_error and one of:

  • lagdynamics_needs_events: the fit was built from a transition matrix, so there are no sequences to split.

  • lagdynamics_bad_input: the fit has fewer than two sequences.

References

Epskamp, S., Borsboom, D., & Fried, E. I. (2018). Estimating psychological networks and their accuracy: A tutorial paper. Behavior Research Methods, 50(1), 195-212.

See also

as.data.frame.lsa_reliability() to read the result; bootstrap_lsa(), certainty_lsa(), stability_lsa() and permute_lsa() for transition-level checks.

Examples

fit <- lsa(engagement)
rel <- reliability_lsa(fit, R = 50)
rel
#> <lsa_reliability>
#>   engine:        classical
#>   replicates:    50
#>   weights:       prob
#>   method:        pearson
#>   n sequences:   136
#>   split-half r:  0.965  (sd = 0.029)
#>   95% CI:        [0.896, 0.997]
#>   failed:        0 of 50 replicates
as.data.frame(rel, what = "summary")
#>   weights  method  R n_failed      mean         sd    ci_low   ci_high
#> 1    prob pearson 50        0 0.9653006 0.02936169 0.8959057 0.9971183

# One result per group
g <- lsa(group_regulation_long, actor = "Actor", action = "Action",
         time = "Time", group = "Achiever")
reliability_lsa(g, R = 20) |>
  as.data.frame(what = "summary")
#>   group weights  method  R n_failed      mean          sd    ci_low   ci_high
#> 1  High    prob pearson 20        0 0.9866562 0.007352071 0.9691266 0.9935066
#> 2   Low    prob pearson 20        0 0.9864346 0.004408260 0.9776246 0.9926271
# \donttest{
# A full analysis uses more splits
reliability_lsa(fit, R = 500)
#> <lsa_reliability>
#>   engine:        classical
#>   replicates:    500
#>   weights:       prob
#>   method:        pearson
#>   n sequences:   136
#>   split-half r:  0.968  (sd = 0.027)
#>   95% CI:        [0.895, 0.996]
#>   failed:        0 of 500 replicates
# }
